title: Critical speed and D′ for runners
goal: Calculate critical speed and D′ from race times and use them, with their limits, to pace track races and marathons and to judge race predictions such as Riegel's.

steps.title: Critical speed and D′
steps.text:
Runners use the same model with speed. [Critical speed](g:critical-speed) (CS, m·s⁻¹) is the asymptote, and [D′](g:d-prime) ("D prime", m) is a fixed distance you can run above CS [[c:cs-def]].

The work–time line becomes a distance–time line:

**distance = CS × t + D′**

Plot race or trial distances against their times: the slope is CS and the intercept D′. For Haile Gebrselassie's best times from 2 to 15 km the line was almost perfect (R² > 0.999, where 1 is a perfect line), giving CS 5.91 m·s⁻¹ and D′ 351 m [[c:geb]].

CS from training data, time trials or a 3-min all-out test agreed and repeated well; D′ did not [[c:dprime-noisy]].

claims.text: In running the CP model uses critical speed (m·s⁻¹) and D′ (m) in place of CP and W′.

evidence.quote: Here though, the terms critical speed (CS)—or critical velocity (CV), as appropriate—and D′, measured in units of m s−1 and m, respectively, are used instead of CP and W′.

claims.text: Distance against time for Gebrselassie's 2–15 km bests was almost perfectly linear (R² > 0.999): CS 5.91 m·s⁻¹, D′ 351 m.

evidence.quote: When distance (between 2 and 15 km) is plotted against time taken to complete the distance, it can be seen that the relationship is highly linear (R2 > 0.999), with CS being estimated as 5.91 m s−1 and D′ estimated as 351 m.

claims.text: In recreational runners, CS from training data, time trials and 3-min all-out tests agreed, and repeat 3-min tests gave excellent reliability for CS; D′ agreed poorly and was only moderately reliable.

evidence.quote: These data suggest that estimations of CS/CP can be derived remotely, from either HAB, TT, or 3MT, although the lower agreement between D'/W' warrants caution when using these measures interchangeably.
Limited agreement existed between estimates of D'/W'. Moderate reliability of D'/W' was demonstrated between the first and second 3MTs, whereas excellent reliability was demonstrated for CS/CP.

steps.title: CS and D′ from two races
steps.problem: A runner's best 1500 m is 4:00 and her best 5000 m is 17:00. Find her CS and D′.
steps: As a pace: 1,000 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 223 s per km, about 3:43 per km.

steps.title: Marathon pace and CS
steps.text:
The marathon is run below CS, at a fraction that depends on how good you are:

| runners | marathon speed |
|---|---|
| 12 elite men (2:03–2:08) | 96 ± 2% of CS |
| recreational, 2:30 finish | about 93% of CS |
| recreational, 6:00 finish | about 79% of CS |

[[c:elite-96]] [[c:rec-cs]]

In over 25,000 recreational runners, CS came from their best training efforts (400 m to 5 km). Those who ran the first half above about 94% of CS were more likely to slow by over 25% in the second half [[c:fade]].

So estimate CS, pick a fraction that fits your level, and don't run the first half above it.

claims.text: In 12 elite men, marathon speed was 96 ± 2% of critical speed estimated from their 1500 m to 15 km bests.

evidence.quote: The key result of this analysis is that, on average, the elite athletes completed the marathon distance at 96 ± 2% of their CS.

claims.text: Recreational runners ran marathons at about 85% of CS on average, faster runners closer to CS (93% at 2:30, 79% at 6:00).

evidence.quote: Runners completed the marathon at 84.8% ± 13.6% CS, with faster runners competing at speeds closer to CS (93.0% CS for 150 min marathon times vs 78.9% CS for 360 min marathon times).

claims.text: Running the first half of a marathon above about 94% of CS made a large second-half slowdown more likely.

evidence.quote: Runners who completed the first half of the marathon at >94% of their CS, and particularly faster than CS, were more likely to slowdown by more than 25% in the second half of race.

steps.title: Track races and the finishing kick
steps.text:
For races of about 2–15 min (about 1500 m to 5000 m for trained runners), the line predicts the time:

**t = (distance − D′) ÷ CS**

With CS 5.0 m·s⁻¹ and D′ 250 m, 3000 m takes (3,000 − 250) ÷ 5.0 = 550 s, or 9:10.

D′ is the budget for running faster than CS. Spend it in early surges and the finish has nothing left; it makes sense to stay near CS and use D′ only when tactics demand it or in the sprint finish [[c:kick]].

In highly trained runners, CS from 3–15 min track runs matched 10-km race speed, while a treadmill test overestimated it [[c:track-cs]].

claims.text: Avoiding frequent or long excursions above CS, except when tactics demand or in a sprint finish, saves D′.

evidence.quote: From a bioenergetic perspective, avoiding frequent or protracted excursions beyond CS, except perhaps when tactically necessary or in a sprint finish, would seem sensible to prevent utilization of D′

claims.text: In highly trained runners, track-determined CS equalled 10-km race speed, while treadmill CS overpredicted it.

evidence.quote: Track critical speed (293 m*min(-1)) was correlated (r = 0.92, P < 0.001) with race speed (293 m*min(-1)), whereas treadmill critical speed (300 m*min(-1)) had the same correlation but over predicted race performance.

steps.title: Riegel's formula and its limits
steps.text:
The [Riegel formula](g:riegel-formula) predicts a longer race from a shorter one:

**T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06**

The exponent above 1 means you slow a little each time the distance grows. From 10 km in 45:00, the marathon comes out at 45 × 4.2195^1.06 ≈ 45 × 4.60 = 207 min (3:27).

In 2,303 recreational runners it worked well up to the half marathon but gave marathon times at least 10 min too fast for half of them [[c:riegel-marathon]]. Riegel himself gave 1.08 for elites and 1.05–1.06 for older recreational men, so one exponent can't fit everyone [[c:riegel-k]].

CS models do worse when stretched: for long races they overestimate speed [[c:extrapolate]].

claims.text: Riegel's formula was well calibrated up to the half marathon but gave marathon times at least 10 min too fast for half of recreational runners.

evidence.quote: The commonly used Riegel formula for race time prediction was well-calibrated for races up to a half-marathon, but dramatically underestimated marathon time, giving times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners.

claims.text: Riegel reported an exponent of about 1.08 for elite runners and 1.05–1.06 for recreational men aged 40–70.

evidence.quote: Riegel cited a k of 1.08 for elite runners and 1.05 to 1.06 for male recreational runners aged 40 to 70

claims.text: For long races, power-law and logarithmic models extrapolated better than asymptotic (CS-type) models, which overestimated performance.

evidence.quote: The predictions of long-distance performances (maximal running speeds for 30 and 60 min and marathon) by extrapolation of the logarithmic and power-law models were more accurate than the predictions by extrapolation in all the asymptotic models.
The overestimations of these long-distance performances by Morton's model were less important than the overestimations by the other asymptotic models.

steps.title: Half marathon from 10 km
steps.problem: A runner runs 10 km in 45:00. What half-marathon time does Riegel predict?
steps: Without the exponent (45 × 2.110 = 94.9 min) you would assume no slowing at all, about 4 min too fast.

points: Critical speed (m·s⁻¹) and D′ (m) are the running forms of CP and W′: distance = CS × t + D′.
Track races of about 2–15 min: t = (distance − D′) ÷ CS. Save D′ for when tactics demand it or the kick.
Marathons are run below CS: about 96% for elites, 79–93% for recreational runners; a first half above about 94% of CS invites a fade.
Riegel (T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06) works to the half marathon but is often 10+ min too fast for recreational marathoners.
Every model is safest inside the range it was fitted on; stretched to long races, CS models overestimate speed.

variants.stem: In what units are critical speed and D′ given?

options.text: CS in m·s⁻¹, D′ in m
options.why: Right: CS is a speed and D′ a distance, the running forms of a power and an amount of work.

options.text: CS in W, D′ in kJ
options.why: Those are the cycling units, for CP and W′.

options.text: CS in m, D′ in m·s⁻¹
options.why: Swapped: the asymptote is a speed and the budget above it is a distance.

options.text: CS in min per km, D′ in s
options.why: Pace is a common way to show CS, but D′ is a distance, not a time.

variants.stem: A runner's best 1500 m is 5:00 and her best 5000 m is 20:00. What is her CS?

options.why: Right: CS = (d₂ − d₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁).
That is the mean speed of the longer race. It was run above CS too, so it overestimates CS.
That is the mean speed of the shorter race, the fastest of all, far above CS.
This divides total distance by total time: a mean speed, not the slope of the line.

variants.stem: A runner's best 1000 m is 3:00 and his best 5000 m is 18:00. What is his CS?

options.why: Right: CS = (d₂ − d₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁).
That is the mean speed of the longer race. It was run above CS too, so it overestimates CS.
That is the mean speed of the shorter race, the fastest of all, far above CS.
This divides total distance by total time: a mean speed, not the slope of the line.

variants.stem: A runner's CS is 4.0 m·s⁻¹. Her best 1500 m is 5:00. What is her D′?

options.why: Right: D′ = distance − CS × time.
That is the distance covered at CS (CS × t). D′ is what is left over.
That is the whole race distance; most of it was run at CS.

options.text: 5 m
options.why: This divides distance by time: a speed, not a distance.

variants.stem: A runner's CS is 4.5 m·s⁻¹. His best 1000 m is 3:00. What is his D′?

options.why: Right: D′ = distance − CS × time.
That is the distance covered at CS (CS × t). D′ is what is left over.
That is the whole race distance; most of it was run at CS.
This divides distance by time: a speed, not a distance.

variants.stem: A runner's CS is 4.2 m·s⁻¹. She plans her marathon at 90% of CS. What finish time does that give?

options.why: Right: race speed = fraction × CS; time = 42,195 m ÷ speed.
That is the time at 100% of CS, which almost nobody holds for a marathon.
This divides CS by the fraction instead of multiplying, giving a speed above CS.

variants.stem: A triathlete's CS is 3.6 m·s⁻¹. He plans a stand-alone marathon at 85% of CS. What finish time does that give?

options.why: Right: race speed = fraction × CS; time = 42,195 m ÷ speed.
That is the time at 100% of CS, which almost nobody holds for a marathon.
This divides CS by the fraction instead of multiplying, giving a speed above CS.

variants.stem: A runner with CS 4.0 m·s⁻¹ targets a 3:15 marathon, an average of 3.61 m·s⁻¹. Feeling good, she runs the first half at 3.9 m·s⁻¹. What does the CS evidence predict?

options.text: A high risk of a big slowdown: she ran the first half at 97.5% of CS
options.why: Right: first halves above about 94% of CS made a slowdown of over 25% more likely.

options.text: A faster finish: banking time early pays off
options.why: Time banked above about 94% of CS was usually lost, and more, in the second half.

options.text: No problem: she stayed below CS, so D′ was never touched
options.why: Below CS spends no D′, but marathon fatigue builds below CS too; the fraction of CS still matters.

options.text: No problem, since 3.9 m·s⁻¹ is only 8% above goal pace
options.why: The problem is her speed relative to CS, 97.5%, not relative to goal pace.

variants.solution: 3:15 = 11,700 s; 42,195 ÷ 11,700 ≈ 3.61 m·s⁻¹ (90% of CS). First half: 3.9 ÷ 4.0 = 97.5% of CS, above the 94% danger line.

variants.stem: A runner has CS 5.0 m·s⁻¹ and D′ 250 m. What 3000 m time does the model predict?

options.why: Right: t = (distance − D′) ÷ CS.
This runs the whole distance at CS and forgets that D′ lets you go faster.
This adds D′ instead of taking it away, as if D′ were extra distance to cover.

variants.stem: A runner has CS 4.2 m·s⁻¹ and D′ 220 m. What 5000 m time does the model predict?

options.why: Right: t = (distance − D′) ÷ CS.
This runs the whole distance at CS and forgets that D′ lets you go faster.
This adds D′ instead of taking it away, as if D′ were extra distance to cover.

variants.stem: In a 5000 m, a runner can either surge at 2 km to break up the pack or sit just under CS and kick over the last 300 m. Which does the CS model favour, and why?

options.text: Sitting in: just under CS spends no D′, so all of it is there for the kick
options.why: Right: D′ is a fixed budget above CS; early surges spend it and it refills only slowly near CS.

options.text: Surging: D′ refills quickly once she drops back under CS
options.why: Near CS, refill is very slow; a surge mostly just spends D′.

options.text: Either: the same D′ is spent in the end anyway
options.why: Surge plus kick spends more than the kick alone, and she can't spend more than D′.

options.text: Surging: D′ is larger when fresh, so use it early
options.why: D′ is a fixed amount at the start, not a reserve that shrinks unless used.

variants.stem: A runner runs 10 km in 50:00. What half-marathon time does Riegel predict?

options.why: Right: T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06.
This scales time by distance alone, as if you could hold the same speed over the longer race.
This multiplies the ratio by 1.06 instead of raising it to the power 1.06.

variants.stem: A triathlete runs a stand-alone 5 km in 20:00. What 10 km time does Riegel predict?

options.why: Right: T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06.
This scales time by distance alone, as if you could hold the same speed over the longer race.
This multiplies the ratio by 1.06 instead of raising it to the power 1.06.

variants.stem: A recreational runner's half marathon is 1:40:00, so Riegel predicts a 3:28:30 marathon. What is the best advice for her race plan?

options.text: Treat 3:28:30 as optimistic and start a little slower
options.why: Right: for recreational runners Riegel was often 10+ min too fast in the marathon, so starting at its pace risks a fade.

options.text: Trust it: Riegel is well calibrated at every distance
options.why: It was well calibrated only up to the half marathon.

options.text: Aim faster: Riegel is too cautious for recreational runners
options.why: The error ran the other way: predicted marathon times were too fast.

options.text: Use an exponent of 1.00, since marathons are steady
options.why: An exponent of 1 assumes no slowing at all, making the prediction even faster.

variants.stem: A CS model fitted to a runner's 1500 m to 5 km races overestimates her marathon speed. Why?

options.text: It treats CS as holdable for ever, but marathons are run well below CS
options.why: Right: asymptotic models overestimate long races; marathoners run at about 79–96% of CS.

options.text: D′ grows during long races, so the fit is too small
options.why: D′ is a fixed budget; in a marathon it hardly matters.

options.text: The distance–time line is not straight for 1500 m to 5 km
options.why: Over that range the line is almost perfectly straight; the problem is stretching it far beyond.

options.text: CS is a cycling idea that doesn't apply to running
options.why: CS works well for running inside its range; extrapolating is the problem.
